lesson.title: Sides in proportion: sin, cos and tan

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is every side growing while opposite ÷ hypotenuse, adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and opposite ÷ adjacent stay put, when you drag the size handle, and all three changing when you drag the angle.
interactive.title: The growing triangle
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on one right-angled triangle, the growing triangle. Its right angle is at the bottom right and the angle in use, θ (the Greek letter theta), is at the bottom left. A size handle sits on the far corner and an angle handle on the top corner. Small labels name the sides from θ: the hypotenuse is the longest side, across from the right angle; the opposite side is across from θ; the adjacent side is the other one, next to θ. Each side shows its length, and three readouts show opposite ÷ hypotenuse, adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and opposite ÷ adjacent to three decimal places. Dragging the size handle enlarges the triangle, and a small scale label shows how many times bigger than the opening triangle it is, × 2 when the hypotenuse goes from 10 cm to 20 cm. Every side is multiplied by that same number, so the readouts stay put. Dragging the angle handle changes the shape, so they change. A switch moves θ to the top corner, and the opposite and adjacent labels swap, while the hypotenuse stays the same. A full turn is 360° and a right angle is a quarter of it. The angles in a triangle make 180°, and the right angle takes 90°, so the other two share 90°, which makes them complementary, and are each less than 90°, which is called acute: with θ at 30°, the top corner is 60°. An angle between 90° and 180° is obtuse, and a right-angled triangle has none. Growing the triangle keeps its three angles, 90°, θ and 180° − 90° − θ, so it stays the same shape. Later screens name the three ratios sin θ, cos θ and tan θ, with SOH CAH TOA spelled out letter by letter, show a calculator's sin key in degrees mode and in another mode, radians, which a later lesson teaches, and turn the triangle into a conduit offset: the offset depth is the opposite side, the distance between the bends is the hypotenuse, and a readout shows the multiplier 1 ÷ sin θ; the screen says this rule comes from the electrical trade and is near enough rather than exact, as it ignores the curve of each bend. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it: a puzzle offers three answers, a wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? draws the triangle for it.
interactive.ignores: The lengths are example values in centimetres or millimetres, and the readouts are rounded to three decimal places. The angle handle stays between 10° and 80°, as in a right-angled triangle both other angles are less than 90°. The conduit is drawn with sharp corners where a real bend is a curve.

explain.text:
In right-angled triangles with the same angle, the sides keep the same proportions however big the triangle is. Here is why. Two such triangles share the right angle, 90°, and the angle you are using, θ (the Greek letter theta). A triangle's angles make 180°, so their third angles match too, and triangles with the same three angles are the same shape. The big one is the small one enlarged, with every side multiplied by the same number, and as in Proportional reasoning, multiplying both parts of a ratio by the same number leaves it unchanged. So one side divided by another gives the same answer in both.[^3] A full turn is 360°,[^9] and a right angle is a quarter of it. An angle between 90° and 180° is obtuse,[^10] so a right-angled triangle has none: its other two angles share 90°, which makes them complementary,[^11] and each is under 90°, or acute. Name the sides from θ: the hypotenuse is across from the right angle, the opposite side is across from θ, and the adjacent side is the other one, next to θ. In the growing triangle θ is 30°. With a hypotenuse of 10 cm the opposite side is 5 cm, and enlarged to 20 cm it is 10 cm, so opposite ÷ hypotenuse is 0.5 both times.

The angle is what changes the ratio. Turn θ from 30° to 40° and the hypotenuse tips up, so more of its length goes into the height, and opposite ÷ hypotenuse grows to 0.643. Each angle has its own three ratios. Opposite ÷ hypotenuse is the [[sine]] of θ, written sin θ. Adjacent ÷ hypotenuse is its [[cosine]], cos θ, and opposite ÷ adjacent is its [[tangent]], tan θ.[^4] Their first letters make SOH CAH TOA, one way to remember which is which: Sine is Opposite ÷ Hypotenuse, Cosine is Adjacent ÷ Hypotenuse, and Tangent is Opposite ÷ Adjacent. A scientific calculator holds these numbers, and for angles in degrees it should be in degrees mode.[^5] sin 30° = 0.5 is one number that belongs to 30°,[^1] not sin times 30. sin 60° is 0.866, not twice sin 30°. In a right-angled triangle the opposite side is shorter than the hypotenuse, so sin θ is less than 1 there, and sin 60° = 1, twice sin 30°, would make the opposite side as long as the hypotenuse. The sine does not grow in step with the angle. In another mode, radians, which a later lesson teaches, the same keys give sin 30 = −0.988.

So the angle and one side give any other side. Pick the ratio that holds the side you know and the side you want, then rearrange. With θ at 30° and a hypotenuse of 10 cm, the opposite side is 10 × sin 30° = 5 cm. When the hypotenuse is the side you want, it is on the bottom of sin θ = opposite ÷ hypotenuse. Multiply both sides by the hypotenuse and divide both by sin θ, and you have hypotenuse = opposite ÷ sin θ. A conduit offset is this triangle, with the offset depth as the opposite side and the distance between the bends as the hypotenuse.[^6] A 150 mm offset with 30° bends needs 150 ÷ 0.5 = 300 mm between bends. Dividing by sin θ is multiplying by 1 ÷ sin θ, which is the multiplier: 2.0 at 30° and 1.414 at 45°.[^1] Multiplying by sin θ instead gives 150 × 0.5 = 75 mm, shorter than the offset, and the hypotenuse is the longest side. The method is an approximation, because it does not account for the arc of the bend.[^7] In a right-angled triangle, a question with two sides and an angle is one for trigonometry.[^8] With two sides and no angle, Pythagoras, from Geometry fundamentals, finds the third.

The course's puzzle, a supply described as 230 V single-phase and 400 V three-phase,[^2] ends in a triangle with a known angle, and these ratios are what turn that angle into a side. **In right-angled triangles with the same angle, each side divided by another gives the same answer however big the triangle is,[^3] so the angle fixes sin θ, cos θ and tan θ, and the angle and one side give any other side.**

analogy.text: A drawing at 1:50 keeps every length in proportion, so a wall twice as long on paper is twice as long on site. A right-angled triangle with a 30° angle is one shape drawn at any scale: its opposite side is half its hypotenuse whether it is drawn 10 cm long or built 10 m long.
analogy.breaks: A drawing's scale compares the drawing with the real thing, while a trig ratio compares two sides of the same triangle. And sin, cos and tan as side ratios need a right angle, because only a right-angled triangle has a hypotenuse; a later lesson gives the rules for other triangles.

practice.text:
- Mark the right angle and the angle you are using, θ.
- Name the sides from θ: the hypotenuse across from the right angle, the opposite across from θ, the adjacent next to θ.
- Pick the ratio that holds the side you know and the side you want (SOH CAH TOA).
- Write it as an equation. If the side you want is on top, multiply; if it is on the bottom, divide.
- For angles in degrees, set the calculator to degrees mode,[^5] then work it out.
- Check against the drawing: no side is longer than the hypotenuse.

**Rule of thumb:** The hypotenuse is the longest side, so finding it means dividing by a number less than 1, and the answer comes out bigger than the side you started with.

**Worked example:** A 120 mm offset with 30° bends. The offset depth is the opposite side and the distance between bends is the hypotenuse.[^6] sin 30° = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, so hypotenuse = 120 ÷ 0.5 = 240 mm, near enough, as the method ignores the arc of the bend.[^7] The multiplier gives the same, 120 × 2.0 = 240 mm.[^1] 240 mm is longer than 120 mm, as a hypotenuse must be.

**Common mistakes**
- Multiplying where you should divide. 120 × 0.5 = 60 mm is shorter than the offset, so it cannot be the distance between bends.
- Using 2.0 at 45° or 1.414 at 30°. Work it out as 1 ÷ sin θ.[^1]
- A calculator in the wrong mode. If sin 30 shows −0.988, it is not in degrees.[^5]
- Treating sin as a multiplication. sin 60° is 0.866, not 2 × sin 30°.
- Naming the sides from the wrong angle. Opposite and adjacent swap when θ moves to the other corner.

interactive.html:
Grow a right-angled triangle and watch which numbers stay put.

Lengths are examples. Each ratio is one side of the drawn triangle divided by another, and the angle alone sets it.
interactive.title: The growing triangle
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is every side growing while opposite ÷ hypotenuse, adjacent ÷ hypotenuse and opposite ÷ adjacent stay put, when you drag the size handle, and all three changing when you drag the angle.

checks.label: For similar right-angled triangles the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides stay in the same proportion: on the growing triangle each readout, one drawn side divided by another, gives the same answer at every size the handle reaches, and turning the angle changes all three

Sine is the ratio of the opposite side to the hypotenuse, cosine the adjacent side to the hypotenuse, and tangent the opposite side to the adjacent side: the named readouts are worked out from the drawn sides just so at every angle the handle reaches, and the sin θ puzzle accepts only opposite ÷ hypotenuse
For 30 degrees, sin(30) = 0.5, so the multiplier 1/0.5 = 2.0; for 45 degrees, sin(45) = 0.7071, so 1/0.7071 = 1.414: the offset screen's readouts show exactly these, worked out as 1 ÷ sin θ

When you bend an offset the conduit forms a right triangle, the offset depth the vertical side (opposite) and the distance between bends the diagonal (hypotenuse): on both offset screens the depth is marked on the upright side, the distance on the diagonal the conduit runs along, and the distance is the depth ÷ sin θ

Scientific calculators should be in degrees mode for trigonometry: the degrees-mode calculator gives the opposite ÷ hypotenuse of the triangle with that angle, on the sin key screen and in the puzzle after it, and the radians-mode one gives a different number

When the question involves two sides and an angle in a right-angled triangle, trigonometry is used: each puzzle that gives an angle and a side is answered with sin, cos or tan, and the one with two sides and no angle by Pythagoras

The angles of a triangle make 180° and the right angle takes 90°, so the 30° triangle's top corner is 180 − 90 − 30 = 60°; every angle the handle reaches leaves both other corners under 90°, and moving θ to the top corner swaps the opposite and adjacent names while the hypotenuse stays

Every worked number matches the lesson: 5 and 10 cm with 0.5 both times, 0.643 at 40°; 13, 21 and 5 cm; 0.866 and 0.577; 0.6, 0.8 and 0.75; 0.5 and −0.988; 0.866, 1 and −0.305; 300 and 75 mm; 283, 141 and 400 mm; 3.83, 3.21 and 6.53 m; 520 (900 × 0.5774), 450 and 1559 mm; 500 mm
Each puzzle accepts only its right answer, every wrong answer has its own hint and its own red row of working, and before an answer nothing in the picture shows the answer

Every triangle is drawn to scale with a square right angle: its drawn sides are its labelled lengths times one scale, the size handle sits on the far corner and the angle handle on the top corner, and the size label is the hypotenuse ÷ 10 cm

No label sits on another label, a line or a handle, or runs off the picture, on any screen in any state: puzzles answered right, wrong or with Why? open, the triangle at its smallest and largest sizes and angles, θ moved, the 45° offset
Every demonstration has finished within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; each answer, Why?, switch and bend has settled within 1.8 s

applied.problem: "Trigonometry is for a question with two sides and an angle" drops the source's "in a right-angled triangle" and is false after i3 to i8; "should be in degrees mode" stops holding once radians (i5, i6) are used.

The worked example gives 240 mm between bends as exact, though the explanation and its source call the multiplier method an approximation that ignores the arc; the degrees-mode step also needs "for angles in degrees" to stay true after radians.
